content: A micropipe is a type of defect that occurs within a single crystal substrate. This defect is of significant concern to manufacturers of silicon carbide (SiC) substrates, which are widely used in various industries, including power devices for vehicles and high-frequency communication devices. During the production of these materials, the crystal experiences both internal and external stresses, which lead to the formation of defects or dislocations within the atomic lattice. One common type of dislocation is the screw dislocation, which alters successive atomic planes within the crystal lattice into a helical shape. When a screw dislocation propagates through the bulk of the material during the wafer growth process, it results in the formation of a micropipe. A high density of micropipes within a wafer can significantly reduce the yield during the device manufacturing process. Micropipes and screw dislocations in epitaxial layers typically originate from the substrates on which the epitaxy is performed. These dislocations, which have a large Burgers vector, follow the growth direction (c-axis) in silicon carbide boules and substrates, extending into the deposited epitaxial layers. Several factors influence the formation of micropipes and other defects, including growth parameters such as temperature, supersaturation, vapor phase stoichiometry, impurities, and the polarity of the seed surface. Numerous research laboratories in universities and companies are actively working to develop micropipe-free substrates. One notable pioneer in the commercialization of SiC materials and devices is Cree Inc., which announced in May 2007 that it had successfully produced 100-mm (4-inch), zero-micropipe, n-type SiC substrates. This achievement demonstrates that it is possible to eliminate these defects in both large-area wafers and smaller fragments, paving the way for the broader commercialization of microelectronic devices in this field.
